newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Eurotunnel agrees debt deal, shares rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Eurotunnel agrees debt deal, shares rise.

text.p: Eurotunnel Plc said on Thursday it had clinched an agreement with lead banks to restructure its debt, a deal which it said would make it financially secure for the next six years.
The Anglo-French Channel Tunnel operator has now cleared the first major hurdle for restructuring nearly nine billion pounds in debt.

If shareholders and the remaining 225-strong banking syndicate approved the deal, Eurotunnel would be free to concentrate on improving its operating performance, it said. The company said it aimed to make an operating profit in 1997 for the first time in its history.
Eurotunnel, struggling with heavy debts due to cost overruns in building the tunnel, suffered more problems last year when a fire cut its traffic sharply.
The substance of the debt deal is unchanged from terms outlined last October. Shareholders will have the chance to keep the right to 54.5 percent of long-term potential profits.

Co-chairmen Patrick Ponsolle and Robert Malpas said in a statement that Eurotunnel's steering committee of bankers had approved the final debt deal. It would be presented to shareholders and the remaining creditor banks in mid-May.
Eurotunnel was upbeat about its longer-term potential, telling investors in a statement it expected "to increase our market share...one can hardly say it has peaked".

The debt news pushed Eurotunnel shares in London and Paris higher even though its reported a 1996 loss of 685 million pounds ($1.1 billion) compared with a 1995 loss of 924 million pounds before interest and charges were levied.

The loss was in line with expectations so markets focused on the debt development which they saw as positive. The shares rose three pence in London to 72-1/2 pence and three percent to 6.7 francs in Paris.
Shares in rival P&O, which operates cross-channel ferries, slid 11 1/2 pence to 600 on the news that Eurotunnel was on a firmer financial footing to fight for market share.
Eurotunnel's 1996 turnover rose to 448 million pounds from 282 million the year before.
Eurotunnel said the first quarter of 1997 went well, with traffic reaching "very satisfactory levels" and fares stabilising after a price-war with the ferry companies.
Ponsolle and Malpas said "1996 was a good year for the group" despite the fire.
The blaze on November 18, 1996 hit tourist traffic and halted freight traffic, although it is due to resume in mid-June after repairs to the tunnel.

They were confident that the Le Shuttle train service would regain the market share lost due to the fire by the end of 1997. So far, it had recovered 80 percent of the market share achieved before the fire.
Traffic on the Eurostar passenger train service, owned by London and Continental Railways, also rose 25 percent in the first quarter of 1997 from the same time in 1996.
Eurotunnel continued to press for an extension of its franchise to run the tunnel, saying the group would get a major boost if the French and British governments agreed.
So far such moves have been resisted and seen as a back-door subsidy.

A meeting of shareholders had been set for June 24 but Ponsolle said it could be delayed to July 10 if the first meeting failed to attract the 33 percent of shareholders needed under French law to proceed.

"The main merit (of the debt plan) is to ensure the financial stability of the group for the six years to come, allowing the management to focus principally on the improvement of the group's performance," said the chairmen.

They admitted in a letter to investors that shareholders "have been disappointed by the financial performance of the group so far and by the need to envisage a financial restructuring that will dilute their position".
But they added that this deal was "the best possible compromise under the present circumstances".
($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
